title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: I spent the following day roaming through the valley. I stood beside the sources of the Arveiron, which rises from a glacier slowly advancing down from the mountain summit to block the valley. The sheer walls of vast mountains rose before me. The icy cliff of the glacier hung over me. A few shattered pines were scattered around. The solemn silence of this glorious throne room of imperial Nature was broken only by the rushing water, the crash of some great falling fragment, the thunder of an avalanche, or the cracking of the accumulated ice as it split and tore under immutable natural laws — as if it were merely a toy in their hands. These sublime, magnificent scenes gave me the greatest comfort I was capable of receiving. They lifted me above all pettiness and, though they didn't remove my grief, they calmed and softened it. To some degree they also diverted my mind from the thoughts that had consumed me for the past month. I went to bed that night, and my sleep was attended by the grand visions I'd absorbed during the day. They gathered around me — the spotless snowy peak, the glittering spire, the pine forests, the jagged ravine, the eagle soaring among the clouds — and bade me be at peace.

But where had they gone when I woke the next morning? All that had inspired my soul fled with sleep. Dark melancholy clouded every thought. Rain poured in torrents. Thick mist hid the mountain summits, so I couldn't even see my mighty friends. But I would penetrate their misty veil and seek them in their cloudy retreats. What were rain and storm to me? My mule was brought to the door, and I resolved to climb to the top of Montanvert. I remembered the effect the sight of the tremendous, ever-moving glacier had produced on my mind when I'd first seen it. It had filled me with a sublime ecstasy that gave wings to my soul, letting it soar above the dark world to light and joy. The sight of the awesome and majestic in nature had always made my mind solemn and helped me forget the petty cares of life. I decided to go without a guide. I knew the path well, and another person would destroy the solitary grandeur of the scene.

The climb is steep, but the path winds in short, continual turns that let you conquer the mountain's sheer face. The landscape is terrifyingly desolate. In a thousand spots you can see the marks of winter avalanches — trees lying broken and scattered, some completely destroyed, others bent against jutting rocks or leaning on other trees. Higher up, the path crosses snow-filled gullies where stones constantly roll down from above. One is especially dangerous — the slightest sound, even a loud voice, can trigger enough movement in the air to bring rocks crashing down on the speaker. The pines aren't tall or lush, but they're dark and add severity to the scene. I looked down at the valley below. Vast mists rose from the rivers and curled in thick wreaths around the opposite mountains, whose peaks were hidden in uniform clouds. Rain fell from the dark sky, deepening my melancholy. Alas! Why does man boast of feelings more refined than those we see in animals? It only makes us more dependent creatures. If our urges were limited to hunger, thirst, and desire, we might be nearly free. But as it is, we're moved by every passing wind and every chance word or scene.

As Percy Shelley's poem "Mutability" puts it: We rest; a dream has power to poison sleep. We rise; one wandering thought pollutes the day. We feel, conceive, or reason; laugh or weep, Embrace fond woe, or cast our cares away; It is the same: for, be it joy or sorrow, The path of its departure still is free. Man's yesterday may never be like his tomorrow; nothing may endure but mutability — change itself!

It was nearly noon when I reached the top. For some time I sat on the rock overlooking the sea of ice. Mist covered it and the surrounding mountains. Then a breeze scattered the clouds, and I descended onto the glacier. The surface is very uneven — rising like the waves of a stormy sea, dipping into hollows, split by crevasses that plunge deep. The ice field is nearly three miles wide, but I spent almost two hours crossing it. The opposite mountain is a bare, vertical cliff. From where I stood, Montanvert was directly across, about three miles away, and above it rose Mont Blanc in awful majesty. I stayed in a sheltered hollow in the rock, gazing at this stupendous scene. The vast river of ice wound among the surrounding mountains, whose towering peaks hung over its depths. Their icy, glittering summits shone in the sunlight above the clouds. My heart, which had been heavy, swelled with something like joy. I cried out: "Wandering spirits, if you truly wander and do not rest in your narrow graves, grant me this small happiness — or take me as your companion, away from the joys of life."

As I said this, I suddenly saw the figure of a man in the distance, moving toward me with superhuman speed. He bounded over the crevasses in the ice that I'd crossed with caution. As he drew closer, his height seemed to exceed that of any normal person. I was alarmed. Mist came over my eyes and I felt faint, but the cold mountain air quickly revived me. I could see, as the shape came nearer — and the sight was terrible and loathsome — that it was the wretch I had created. I trembled with rage and horror, resolving to wait for him and then engage him in mortal combat. He approached. His face showed bitter anguish combined with contempt and malice, while its inhuman ugliness made it almost too horrible to look at. But I barely noticed. Rage and hatred had first robbed me of speech. When I recovered, I overwhelmed him with words of furious hatred and contempt.

"Devil!" I cried. "How dare you approach me? Don't you fear the fierce vengeance of my arm? Begone, vile insect! Or better — stay, so I can trample you to dust! Oh, if only I could, by destroying your miserable existence, restore the victims you have so fiendishly murdered!"

"I expected this reception," said the demon. "All men hate the wretched. How much more must I be hated — I, who am miserable beyond all living things! Yet you, my creator, despise and reject me, your creature, to whom you're bound by ties that only the destruction of one of us can break. You plan to kill me. How dare you play with life this way? Do your duty toward me, and I'll do mine toward you and the rest of humanity. If you agree to my terms, I'll leave you and everyone else in peace. But if you refuse, I'll gorge the jaws of death with the blood of your remaining friends."

"Loathsome monster! Fiend! The tortures of hell are too mild a punishment for your crimes. Wretched devil! You blame me for creating you? Come, then, and let me extinguish the spark I so carelessly gave you."
My rage was beyond bounds. I sprang at him, driven by every feeling that can arm one being against another.
He easily dodged me and said,

"Calm yourself! I beg you to hear me before you unleash your hatred. Haven't I suffered enough already — must you try to increase my misery? Life, even if it's nothing but an accumulation of pain, is dear to me. I'll defend it. Remember: you made me more powerful than yourself. I'm taller than you, and my joints are more supple. But I won't pit myself against you. I am your creature, and I'll be obedient and docile to my natural lord and king — if you'll also fulfill your obligations to me. Oh, Frankenstein, don't be fair to everyone else and trample on me alone — me, to whom your justice, your mercy, and your love are most owed. Remember that I am your creature. I should be your Adam, but instead I'm the fallen angel, driven from joy for no sin. Everywhere I see happiness, from which I alone am forever excluded. I was good and kind. Misery made me a fiend. Make me happy, and I'll be good again."
"Begone! I won't listen. There can be nothing between us. We are enemies. Leave, or let us fight to the death."

"How can I reach you? Won't any plea make you look on your creature with kindness? Believe me, Frankenstein — I was good. My soul glowed with love and compassion. But am I not alone, miserably alone? You, my creator, despise me. What hope can I find in your fellow humans, who owe me nothing? They reject and hate me. The barren mountains and empty glaciers are my refuge. I've wandered here for days. The ice caves, which I alone don't fear, are my home — the only one that no human grudges me. I welcome these bleak skies because they're kinder to me than people. If all humanity knew I existed, they would arm themselves against me as you do. Shouldn't I hate those who hate me? I won't keep peace with my enemies. I'm miserable, and they'll share my misery. Yet it is in your power to make amends to me and to save them from an evil — an evil that you alone can let grow so great that not only you and your family, but thousands of others, will be swallowed up in the whirlwinds of its rage. Let your compassion be stirred, and don't reject me. Listen to my story. When you've heard it, abandon me or pity me, as you judge I deserve. But hear me. The guilty are allowed, by human laws, bloody as they are, to speak in their own defense before they're condemned. Listen to me, Frankenstein. You accuse me of murder, yet you would destroy your own creation with a clear conscience. Oh, praise the eternal justice of man! But I don't ask you to spare me. Just listen to me. Then, if you can, and if you will, destroy the work of your hands."

"Why do you remind me," I replied, "of things I shudder to recall — that I was the miserable cause and author of all this? Cursed be the day, loathsome devil, that you first saw light! Cursed — though I curse myself — be the hands that formed you! You've made me wretched beyond words. You've left me no power even to consider whether I am being just to you or not. Get out! Remove your hated form from my sight."

"Then I'll remove it, my creator," he said, and placed his despised hands over my eyes. I flung them away violently. "This way I spare you a sight you hate. But you can still listen. Grant me your compassion. By the goodness I once possessed, I demand this. Hear my tale. It's long and strange, and this place is too cold for your delicate constitution. Come to the hut on the mountain. The sun is still high. Before it sets behind these snowy peaks to light another world, you'll have heard my story and can decide. It rests with you whether I leave the company of men forever and live a harmless life, or become the scourge of your fellow creatures and the architect of your own swift destruction."

As he said this, he led the way across the ice. I followed. My heart was full, and I didn't answer. But as we walked, I weighed the various arguments he'd made and decided at least to listen to his tale. I was partly driven by curiosity, and compassion confirmed my decision. Until now I'd assumed he'd murdered my brother, and I was desperate for confirmation or denial. For the first time, I also felt what duties a creator owes to his creation — that I should make him happy before complaining of his wickedness. These reasons convinced me to agree. We crossed the ice and climbed the opposite rock. The air was cold, and rain began again. We entered the hut. The fiend wore an air of triumph. I entered with a heavy heart and crushed spirits. But I agreed to listen. I sat down by the fire my detestable companion had lit, and he began his tale.
